sections.heading: Devnet 11 and Devnet 8 Status
sections.summary: Devnet 11 Glamsterdam activation went smoothly; devnet 8 recovered from JUMP attack but Besu still struggles with TSTORE spam.
sections.body:
- Devnet 11 activated Glamsterdam on Monday with no participation drop and all clients following the chain correctly.
  - Lido and Optimism deployed their stacks and reported everything went well.
  - Network will be kept up for about one more week, then shut down; primary testing continues on devnet 8.
- Devnet 8 experienced a JUMP attack earlier in the week that heavily affected Besu nodes; the attack was stopped and most nodes recovered.
  - Besu required SnapSync to recover from persistent out-of-memory issues.
  - Lighthouse block production issues and a Reth gas-limit mismatch occurred but were resolved by deploying correct images.
- An unknown entity began TSTORE spamming on devnet 8, causing Besu block import times of ~7 seconds (~20 megagas/second).
  - Besu team (Justin Florentine) confirmed awareness and has two PRs in flight to address the issues.

sections.heading: MPLEX Deprecation and QUIC Defaults
sections.summary: Agreement to ship Glamsterdam with QUIC enabled by default on all clients; MPLEX removal deferred to the first release after Glamsterdam activation.
sections.body:
- Teku reported QUIC is already enabled by default but does not want to remove MPLEX or TCP before Glamsterdam ships, citing lack of data on how many users have properly configured QUIC networking.
- Daniel Knopik expressed frustration that MPLEX deprecation has been discussed for three years and was previously agreed for Glamsterdam, yet is being delayed again.
  - Clarified that deprecating MPLEX does not equal deprecating TCP, since TCP + Yamux remains an option.
- Agreement reached: all clients will ship QUIC enabled by default with Glamsterdam releases.
  - Teku suggested adding a warning log for nodes without active QUIC peers, encouraging users to check their configuration before TCP is removed.
  - After Glamsterdam activates, clients are free to remove MPLEX support in subsequent releases.
- Consensus-specs [PR 3866](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/3866) (formally deprecating MPLEX) will be merged after Glamsterdam is live.

sections.heading: Sepolia Fork Date and Client Releases
sections.summary: Sepolia Glamsterdam fork confirmed for October 6th; client releases requested by September 29th at the latest, ideally sooner.
sections.body:
- The Sepolia Glamsterdam fork date of October 6th was confirmed with no objections.
- Blog post, eth-clients repo updates, and meta EIP updates will be handled by stokes today or tomorrow.
- Client teams asked to get releases out as soon as possible; absolute deadline is September 29th (one week before fork), but earlier is strongly preferred.
  - Terence noted Sepolia is fairly centralized, so one week lead time is likely sufficient.
- Fredrik flagged that this shorter timeline bypasses the protocol upgrade process requirement of 14 days between release-ready clients and testnet activation.
  - The 14-day window is used for internal security reviews and adding releases to the bug bounty program.
  - Accepted as a reasonable tradeoff for Sepolia given its centralized nature; client teams urged to release early to maximize review time.
- Fredrik confirmed that releases can be added to the bug bounty program as soon as they are ready.

sections.heading: Builder Circuit Breakers for Testnets
sections.summary: Potuz urged all CL clients to implement robust builder circuit breakers before Sepolia, since testnet builders can be cheaply spoofed to DOS the chain.
sections.body:
- Potuz warned that on testnets, where ETH is free, anyone can spin up many fake builders, offer high bids, and fail to produce payloads, effectively DOSing the chain at zero cost.
  - Current circuit breakers in most clients fall back to local building only after many missed blocks, which is insufficient.
- Toni Wahrstätter questioned why testnet circuit breakers should be stricter than mainnet, noting he uses builders on devnets for EL testing.
  - Potuz clarified the difference: on mainnet, buying and wasting a block costs real ETH; on testnets, it's free and trivially scalable.
- Potuz also raised the broader concern that major production builders (Titan, Ultrasound, etc.) have not been tested through the fork transition on devnets.
  - Asked that testing with production builders happen on the public testnets before mainnet; stokes said this should definitely happen on Hoodi, and on Sepolia if it can be pulled together.
  - In chat, potuz argued Sepolia is the better venue since most validators can be made to connect to builder endpoints, while pk910 noted Sepolia's gated deposit contract blocks early builder deposits (fine on Hoodi).
  - potuz was unsure how many CL clients actively call the Builder API; he believed Prysm and Lodestar do, others unclear.
- Teku (Stefan Bratanov) confirmed Builder API support is in place for Sepolia.

sections.heading: Hoodi Fork Planning
sections.summary: Hoodi fork tentatively targeted for October 27th, pending Sepolia success; confirmation expected at the October 8th ACD call.
sections.body:
- Stokes proposed scheduling the Hoodi fork ~3 weeks after Sepolia, around October 26-27.
- Lodestar (Matthew Keil) requested waiting until Sepolia goes smoothly before committing to a Hoodi date, supported by several teams.
- Proposed plan: prepare all Hoodi-related PRs and resources by October 1st; fork Sepolia on the 6th; confirm Hoodi on the October 8th ACD call if Sepolia is clean.
  - Client releases for Hoodi would target October 13th, giving two weeks before the October 27th fork.
- Stokes strongly advised against scheduling the Hoodi fork during Devcon week, citing past experience with fork issues disrupting the conference.
- The plan for Hoodi also incorporates builder testing: major builders should be deposited and active before the fork so the relay path is tested with real production software.
- No objections to this tentative plan; thumbs up received from multiple participants.
- Stokes noted that mainnet scheduling will only happen after both Sepolia and Hoodi are observed to be healthy.

sections.heading: EIP-8411 PFI Request (Fast Execution Payload Broadcast)
sections.summary: EIP-8411 accepted as PFI for Hegota; clients asked to add it to their rankings before next call, with CFI decision deferred.
sections.body:
- Kamil Salakhiev presented [EIP-8411](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12299), a new EIP for fast execution payload broadcast via chunked gossip.
  - Evolved from Block-in-Blobs (EIP-8142) but scoped down: no erasure coding, no new subnets, no reuse of data column subnets.
  - Splits execution payloads into 64 chunks with a Merkle tree commitment included in the bid; attaches Merkle proofs to each chunk.
  - Simulation results: P95 latency for 1MB payload broadcast drops from ~6 seconds to ~2 seconds across 4,000 hosts.
- Motivation: gossip-sub is inefficient for large messages due to store-and-forward delay and in-flight duplicates; Glamsterdam gas limit increase and potential quick slots make this more urgent.
  - Post-Glamsterdam congestion at 300 MGas is expected to produce ~2MB payloads regularly (per potuz).
- Toni Wahrstätter supported inclusion, noting in chat that it consumes much of the value of BAL sidecars, especially if shipped with an earlier BAL deadline, and is a big gain.
- Ansgar Dietrichs suggested PFI is reasonable but asked that the CFI decision be made after all other pending CFI decisions, to allow proper analysis of complexity and forward compatibility.
  - Multiple thumbs up on this approach.
- Erasure coding can be added later in a separate EIP; the current design is forward-compatible.
- Potuz noted the spec change is straightforward and implementation without erasure coding is simple; no need for dedicated breakouts yet.
- Kamil shared relevant [Discord thread](https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/1545447655759544330) and [ethresear.ch post](https://ethresear.ch/t/eip-8411-what-segmented-payload-diffusion-is-made-of/26025) for further discussion.
- Decision: PFI approved; clients to update their rankings with EIP-8411 before the next call.

sections.heading: EIP-8015 CFI (Removal of Unused Beacon State Fields)
sections.summary: EIP-8015 CFI'd for Hegota with no objections; removes beacon state fields that are not written to today.
sections.body:
- EIP-8015, authored by Terence and Etan, removes beacon state fields that currently serve no function.
- Strong client support across all rankings; no objections raised.
- Decision: CFI'd for Hegota.

sections.heading: EIP-8365 Scope Reduction (BLS Withdrawal Credential Retirement)
sections.summary: Consensus to CFI EIP-8365 with reduced scope (deposit guard only, no forced exits); updated EIP expected by next call for formal CFI.
sections.body:
- EIP-8365 currently includes two parts: (1) blocking new 0x00 BLS deposits (deposit guard) and (2) forced exits of existing 0x00 validators.
- Terence clarified Prysm's ranking was A-tier only for part 1; with forced exits included, it would be DFI. Lighthouse expressed the same view.
- Strong consensus from multiple teams against forced exits in Hegota:
  - Potuz argued the standard deprecation procedure is: first stop accepting deposits, then force exits in a future fork.
  - Approximately 8,975 active 0x00 validators remain; many are believed to be stolen keys still earning rewards, deserving time to attempt recovery.
  - NC noted in chat that the current EIP design exits 1 0x00 validator per epoch, taking ~2 months to complete.
- Potuz noted 0x00 withdrawal credentials are likely PQ-safe since their BLS keys have never signed a public message; no urgency to force-exit before PQ.
- Matthew Keil proposed writing both phases into the EIP: Hegota for closing deposits, I-Star for forced exits, providing a documented timeline.
  - Greg K (Lido) suggested also hardcoding a future epoch for forced exits to prevent backtracking.
  - Potuz supported hardcoding as an option but preferred next-fork approach.
- Kevaundray Wedderburn confirmed a PR already exists with the scope reduction.
- Decision: strong lean toward CFI with reduced scope (deposit guard only); EIP update to be merged before next call, with formal CFI expected at that time.

sections.heading: Hegota DFI Batch and PQ Roadmap
sections.summary: Seven CL EIPs DFI'd in bulk; hash-chain RANDAO (8321) DFI'd but PQ preparatory work acknowledged as important during Hegota.
sections.body:
- Stokes proposed DFI-ing all EIPs with average client ranking scores at or below ~0.4 (red box on forkcast), excluding issuance (EIP-8363).
- The following EIPs were DFI'd with no objections: 8237, 8341, 8367, 8321 (hash-chain RANDAO), 8243, 8146, 8375.
  - Justin Traglia's "DFI them all" in chat drew broad thumbs-up agreement from client and research participants.
- EIP-8321 (hash-chain RANDAO) discussion:
  - Kevaundray Wedderburn acknowledged DFI but asked that PQ preparatory work be done during Hegota to ensure readiness for I-Star.
  - Key concern: all validators should have PQ key material registered on the beacon chain as a hedge against earlier-than-expected quantum threats.
  - Dustin noted hash-chain RANDAO locks in specific algorithms and can be done later without being rate-limiting.
- EIP-8369 (FOCIL/Frames interaction, informational): no formal decision needed since it is informational and was not included in client rankings.
  - soispoke asked that teams acknowledge the need to converge FOCIL and Frames specs; general agreement this will be addressed in existing breakout calls.
- EIP-8333 (Align Checkpoint with Epoch Boundary Block): Kevaundray Wedderburn and Matthew Keil both suggested DFI, citing prior telegraphing that it would no longer be relevant in a decoupled consensus world. Ben Edgington agreed but asked to hold the decision until the next call given the call was over time; stokes concurred.

sections.heading: EIP-8363 Issuance Change
sections.summary: Issuance EIP tabled for today; stokes committed to proposing a decision-making process by next call, acknowledging this requires broader community input.
sections.body:
- Stokes proposed tabling EIP-8363 (issuance reduction) due to its unique community-wide impact and the call running over time.
  - Three client teams ranked it DFI; three teams abstained entirely, reflecting inability rather than unwillingness to decide.
- Potuz argued the situation is unfair: affected community members (stakers) are overwhelmingly against, while only researcher arguments in favor have been presented; core devs lack the expertise for monetary policy decisions.
  - Suggested the EIP authors bring in experts from outside the community (e.g., people working on monetary policy) to provide less biased analysis.
- Ansgar Dietrichs stressed this is not a conspiracy to delay-and-squeeze; the real issue is that no decision-making framework exists for this type of EIP.
  - Stated it is "quite clear that we are very far away from any scenario in which this would go into Hegota."
  - Argued against a quick DFI because the same governance gap would recur with future similar proposals.
- lightclient argued for DFI-ing now to avoid the appearance of legitimizing the change while the process is being figured out; the governance discussion can happen separately.
- Enrico Del Fante echoed potuz, saying this needs dedicated calls with non-technical stakeholders; two weeks won't change the situation.
- Greg K (Lido) asked what concrete next steps would look like, noting the current trajectory risks repeating the same inconclusive discussion.
- Jerome de Tychey (EIP author side) acknowledged the need for broader consensus and committed to working on a proper write-up and stakeholder engagement.
- knoshua noted there are people who want an issuance change but disagree with EIP-8363's specifics, so leaving it hanging has its own costs.
- Decision: tabled for today. Stokes committed to proposing a decision-making process by the next call. No DFI or CFI decision made.
